# Database Transaction Recovery After Power Failure

A power failure is one of the most demanding failure scenarios a database system must survive. Unlike a clean shutdown, a power loss gives the database no opportunity to flush in-memory state, write final log records, or update metadata. Recovery must therefore reconstruct a consistent state from whatever durable artifacts survived on disk. This article explains the mechanisms used, walks through concrete worked examples, and discusses the limitations that remain even in well-engineered systems.

## 1. The Core Problem: Atomicity and Durability

A transaction is expected to satisfy ACID properties. Two of these are directly threatened by power loss

The idea is simple: if a program computes the same value more than once, and nothing has changed between the computations, the compiler can compute it once and reuse the result. # How TCP Congestion Control Adapts to Changing Bandwidth

TCP congestion control is the set of algorithms that governs how aggressively a sender injects packets into the network, and how it backs off when the network signals distress. The central challenge it addresses is that a TCP sender has no direct knowledge of the available bandwidth along its path—it must infer it from observable feedback: acknowledgments arriving, round-trip times changing, and (in modern variants) explicit signals from routers.
